lab_title: Cardiac Anatomy and Circulation: Exploring the Human Heart
top_level_objectives: Identify the four chambers and four valves of the human heart and explain their structural relationships
Trace the complete path of blood through the heart chambers and major vessels during one cardiac cycle
Understand the anatomical basis for the structural differences between the right and left ventricles and their functional consequences
Explain how cardiac valves prevent backflow and maintain unidirectional blood flow through the heart

scenes.brief_purpose: Students gain initial familiarity with the gross anatomy of the heart, identify the four chambers in their anatomical positions, and observe the relative size differences between atria and ventricles.
key_visuals: Anterior and posterior views of an intact human heart
Color-coded chambers (right atrium and ventricle in one color, left atrium and ventricle in another)
Labels identifying the four chambers
Clear demonstration of the substantially larger left ventricle
student_actions: Rotate and manipulate a 3D heart model to view it from multiple angles
Tap on each chamber to highlight it and hear its name
Observe and note the relative sizes and wall thicknesses of the ventricles

scenes.brief_purpose: Students locate and identify the four cardiac valves, understand their anatomical positions between chambers and between chambers and vessels, and observe their basic structure.
key_visuals: Cross-sectional or partially transparent view of the heart showing valve locations
Individual valve structures highlighted in sequence (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic)
Anatomical labels and brief descriptions of valve location
Visual distinction between atrioventricular valves (with chordae tendineae) and semilunar valves
student_actions: Tap on each valve to highlight and identify it
Match each valve name to its correct location between chambers
Observe the structural differences between atrioventricular and semilunar valve types

scenes.scene_name: Major Vessels: Entry and Exit Routes
scenes.brief_purpose: Students identify the six major vessels connected to the heart, understand whether each carries deoxygenated or oxygenated blood, and trace their anatomical connections to the heart chambers.
key_visuals: Heart with all major vessels displayed and labeled: superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries (left and right), pulmonary veins (left and right), and aorta
Color coding to indicate deoxygenated blood (dark blue) and oxygenated blood (bright red)
Clear attachment points showing which vessels connect to which chambers
student_actions: Identify each vessel by name and trace its path to or from the heart
Classify each vessel as carrying deoxygenated or oxygenated blood
Predict the chamber(s) each vessel connects to before confirming with visual feedback

scenes.scene_name: Systemic Circulation: The Path of Deoxygenated Blood
scenes.brief_purpose: Students trace deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation through the right heart and into the pulmonary circulation, understanding how the right side receives and pumps venous return.
key_visuals: Animated blood flow beginning from the venae cavae
Progressive highlighting of the right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, and pulmonary valve
Deoxygenated blood (dark blue) flowing from body tissues through venae cavae into right atrium
Pulmonary arteries showing flow of deoxygenated blood leaving the right ventricle toward the lungs
student_actions: Follow the step-by-step animation of deoxygenated blood through the right heart
Identify the chambers and valves blood passes through in order
Explain why the deoxygenated blood must reach the lungs before returning to the left heart

scenes.scene_name: Pulmonary Circulation: Gas Exchange and Return
scenes.brief_purpose: Students understand the role of the lungs in oxygenating blood and observe the path of newly oxygenated blood returning to the left heart via the pulmonary veins.
key_visuals: Animated representation of gas exchange in the lungs
Pulmonary arteries showing deoxygenated blood entering the lungs
Pulmonary veins showing oxygenated blood (bright red) returning from the lungs
Progressive highlighting of the left atrium receiving the oxygenated blood
student_actions: Observe the gas exchange process in simplified form within the lung representation
Trace oxygenated blood from pulmonary veins into the left atrium
Explain the functional difference between pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins (vessel type vs. blood oxygenation)

scenes.scene_name: Systemic Ejection: The Left Heart and Aortic Circulation
scenes.brief_purpose: Students trace oxygenated blood from the left atrium through the left ventricle and into the aorta, understanding how the powerful left ventricle distributes blood throughout the entire body.
key_visuals: Animated blood flow through the left atrium and mitral valve
Left ventricle with visibly thicker myocardium compared to right ventricle
Mitral valve opening to allow filling and closing to prevent backflow
Aortic valve opening and blood flowing into the aorta
Aorta branching and carrying oxygenated blood to systemic tissues
student_actions: Follow the animation of oxygenated blood through left heart chambers and valves
Compare the wall thickness and structure of left versus right ventricles
Explain why the left ventricle is muscularly thicker and more powerful

scenes.scene_name: Complete Cardiac Cycle: Integrated Blood Flow
scenes.brief_purpose: Students synthesize their understanding by observing the complete, simultaneous flow of blood through both circuits of the heart during one full cardiac cycle, reinforcing the dual-loop nature of circulation.
key_visuals: Full heart model with simultaneous animation of blood flow through all chambers and vessels
Color-coded blood showing deoxygenated (dark blue) and oxygenated (red) blood on different pathways
All four valves shown opening and closing in proper sequence
Timeline or indicator showing the stage of the cardiac cycle (atrial systole, ventricular systole, diastole)
student_actions: Observe the complete cardiac cycle without stopping, noting the timing and coordination of all events
Pause the animation at key moments (atrial systole, ventricular systole, diastole) to verify valve positions
Describe the complete path of one oxygen molecule from systemic tissues, through the heart, to the lungs, back through the heart, and to new systemic tissues

scenes.brief_purpose: Students understand the critical role of cardiac valves in maintaining unidirectional flow and explore what happens when valves fail to seal properly, reinforcing the structure-function relationship.
key_visuals: Close-up, detailed views of each valve during opening and closing phases
Animation showing how valve flaps or cusps seal to prevent backflow
Simplified representation of chordae tendineae in atrioventricular valves preventing eversion
Comparison view: normal valve closure (preventing backflow) versus incompetent valve (allowing regurgitation)
student_actions: Examine each valve type in detail and describe its structure
Predict what happens if the mitral valve fails to close completely during ventricular systole
Explain how the valves maintain unidirectional flow despite pressure changes during the cardiac cycle
